title: VI. Why Is Such A Man Alive?
paragraphs: Dmitri Fyodorovitch was twenty-eight, a man of medium height and pleasant looks, though he seemed older than he was. He was muscular, and clearly very strong. Yet his face did not look healthy. It was rather thin, the cheeks were hollow, and their color was an unwholesome yellow. His large, dark, prominent eyes were firm and determined, and yet there was something vague in them as well. Even when he was worked up and talking angrily, his eyes somehow did not follow his mood. They gave away something else, at times quite at odds with what was happening. “You can’t tell what he’s thinking,” people who spoke with him would sometimes say. Those who read something brooding and sullen in his eyes were startled when he suddenly laughed, since the laugh showed that cheerful, light-hearted thoughts were in his mind just when his eyes looked so gloomy. The strained look on his face just now was easy to understand. Everyone knew, or had heard, what a wild and dissolute life he had been leading lately, and how violently angry he had become in his quarrels with his father. Several stories about it were going around town. It is true that he was hot-tempered by nature, “of an unstable and unbalanced mind,” as our justice of the peace, Katchalnikov, aptly put it.

He was dressed stylishly and impeccably, in a frock-coat buttoned up with care. He wore black gloves and carried a top hat. He had only recently left the army, so he still wore a mustache and no beard. His dark brown hair was cropped short and combed forward over his temples. He strode in the long, determined way of a soldier. He paused for a moment on the threshold and looked over the whole company. Then he guessed that the elder was their host, went straight to him, bowed low and asked for his blessing. Father Zossima rose in his chair and blessed him. Dmitri kissed his hand respectfully and said, with deep feeling, almost with anger:

“Please be generous enough to forgive me for keeping you waiting so long. Smerdyakov, the servant my father sent me, told me twice, when I asked him, that the appointment was for one o’clock. And now I suddenly find out—”
“Don’t upset yourself,” the elder interrupted. “It’s nothing. You are a little late, that’s all. It makes no difference....”
“I’m very grateful to you. I expected no less from your kindness.”

With that, Dmitri bowed again. Then he turned abruptly to his father and gave him a bow just as low and respectful. He had plainly planned it beforehand, and he made this bow in all seriousness, feeling it was his duty to show respect and good intentions.

Fyodor Pavlovitch was taken by surprise, but he rose to the occasion. He jumped up from his chair and answered Dmitri’s bow with an equally deep one. His face turned suddenly solemn and impressive, which made him look positively spiteful. Dmitri bowed once to everyone present. Then, without a word, he crossed to the window with his long, resolute stride and sat on the one empty chair, next to Father Païssy. He leaned forward, ready to listen to the conversation he had broken off.
Dmitri’s entrance had taken no more than two minutes, and the talk picked up again. But this time Miüsov did not think it worth answering Father Païssy’s insistent and almost irritable question.

“Please let me step out of this discussion,” he said, with a touch of well-bred indifference. “It’s a subtle question anyway. Look, Ivan Fyodorovitch is smiling at us. He must have something interesting to say on it too. Ask him.”

“Nothing special, only one small remark,” Ivan answered at once. “European Liberals in general, and even our own liberal amateurs, often mix up the end results of socialism with those of Christianity. This wild idea is, of course, typical of them. But it isn’t only Liberals and amateurs who mix up socialism and Christianity. In many cases, it seems, the police do it too—the foreign police, naturally. Your Paris anecdote fits rather well, Pyotr Alexandrovitch.”

“Let me ask your permission to drop this subject altogether,” Miüsov repeated. “Instead, gentlemen, I’ll tell you another interesting and fairly typical story about Ivan Fyodorovitch himself. Just five days ago, at a gathering here, mostly of ladies, he solemnly declared in the middle of an argument that nothing in the whole world makes people love their neighbors. He said there is no natural law that man should love mankind. If there has been any love on earth up to now, he said, it was not because of a natural law but only because men have believed in immortality. Ivan Fyodorovitch added in passing that the whole of natural law rests on that belief. Destroy mankind’s faith in immortality, he said, and not only love but every living force that keeps the world going would dry up at once. Moreover, nothing would be immoral then, and everything would be lawful, even cannibalism. And that’s not all. He finished by claiming that for every individual like ourselves, who believes neither in God nor in immortality, the natural moral law must at once turn into the exact opposite of the old religious law. Egoism, even to the point of crime, would become not merely lawful but recognized as the inevitable, the most rational, even the most honorable outcome of his situation. From this one paradox, gentlemen, you can judge the rest of the theories of our eccentric and paradoxical friend Ivan Fyodorovitch.”
“Excuse me,” Dmitri suddenly cried out, “did I hear right? Crime must not only be allowed but recognized as the inevitable and most rational outcome, for every unbeliever! Is that it, or not?”
“Exactly,” said Father Païssy.
“I’ll remember that.”
With these words Dmitri fell silent, as abruptly as he had spoken up. Everyone looked at him curiously.
“Do you really hold that conviction about what follows if faith in immortality disappears?” the elder suddenly asked Ivan.
“Yes, that was my argument. There is no virtue without immortality.”
“Blessed are you if you believe that. Or else you are most unhappy.”
“Why unhappy?” Ivan asked with a smile.
“Because most likely you do not believe in the immortality of your own soul, nor in what you wrote yourself in your article on Church jurisdiction.”
“Maybe you’re right! ... But I wasn’t entirely joking,” Ivan said suddenly, strangely, and flushed quickly as he did.

“You were not entirely joking. That is true. The question still gnaws at your heart, and you have not answered it. But a man in torment sometimes likes to play with his despair, as if despair itself had driven him to it. In your despair you play with it too, with magazine articles and talk in society. You do not believe your own arguments, and with an aching heart you laugh at them inwardly.... That question you have not answered, and it is your great grief, for it demands an answer.”
“But can I answer it? Can it be answered in the affirmative?” Ivan went on asking in the same strange way, still looking at the elder with the same unexplained smile.

“If it cannot be settled in the affirmative, it will never be settled in the negative. You know that this is the peculiarity of your heart, and all its suffering comes from that. But thank the Creator, who gave you a lofty heart, able to suffer so, able to think and to seek higher things, for our dwelling is in the heavens. May God grant that your heart finds the answer while you are still on earth, and may God bless your path.”

The elder raised his hand, meaning to make the sign of the cross over Ivan from where he stood. But Ivan got up from his seat, went to him, took his blessing, kissed his hand, and returned to his place without a word. His face was firm and earnest. This gesture, and the whole conversation before it, so surprising coming from Ivan, struck everyone as strange and somehow solemn. They all stayed silent for a moment, and Alyosha’s face showed something close to alarm. But Miüsov suddenly shrugged. And at that same moment Fyodor Pavlovitch sprang up from his seat.

“Most pious and holy elder,” he cried, pointing at Ivan, “that is my son, flesh of my flesh, the dearest of my flesh! He is my most dutiful Karl Moor, so to speak. This other son, who has just come in, Dmitri, the one I’m asking you to give me justice against, is the undutiful Franz Moor. They’re both out of Schiller’s _Robbers_, and that makes me the reigning Count von Moor! Judge us and save us! We need not only your prayers but your prophecies!”
“Speak without buffoonery, and don’t begin by insulting your own family,” answered the elder, in a weak, worn-out voice. He was plainly growing more and more tired, and his strength was failing.

“A disgraceful farce, and I knew it would come to this when I came here!” cried Dmitri indignantly. He too jumped to his feet. “Forgive it, reverend Father,” he added, turning to the elder. “I’m not a cultured man and I don’t even know how to address you properly. But you’ve been deceived, and you were too kind-hearted to let us meet here. All my father wants is a scandal. Why he wants it, only he can say. He always has his reasons. But I think I know why—”

“They all blame me, all of them!” cried Fyodor Pavlovitch in his turn. “Pyotr Alexandrovitch here blames me too. You’ve been blaming me, Pyotr Alexandrovitch, you have!” he said, rounding suddenly on Miüsov, who had no thought of interrupting him. “They all accuse me of hiding the children’s money in my boots and cheating them. But isn’t there a court of law? There they’ll add it all up for you, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, from your notes, your letters and your agreements: how much money you had, how much you’ve spent, how much you’ve got left. Why does Pyotr Alexandrovitch refuse to give judgment? Dmitri is no stranger to him. Because they’re all against me, that’s why, while Dmitri Fyodorovitch owes me money, and not a little, but some thousands, and I have the papers to prove it. The whole town is echoing with his debauchery. And at his old post, more than once he spent a thousand or two on seducing some respectable girl. We know all about that, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, down to the most secret details. I’ll prove it.... Would you believe it, holy Father, he has captured the heart of the most honorable of young ladies, from a good family, with money of her own, the daughter of a gallant colonel who had once been his superior officer, a man who had won many honors and wore the Anna Order on his chest. He compromised the girl with a promise to marry her. Now she’s an orphan, and she’s here, and she’s engaged to him. And yet right in front of her he’s dancing attendance on a certain enchantress. And although this enchantress has lived, so to speak, in a civil marriage with a respectable man, still she has an independent character and is an unapproachable fortress to everyone, just like a lawful wife—for she is virtuous, yes, holy Fathers, she is virtuous. Dmitri Fyodorovitch wants to open this fortress with a golden key. That’s why he’s so insolent to me now and tries to squeeze money out of me, though he’s already thrown away thousands on this enchantress. He’s forever borrowing for the purpose. From whom, do you think? Shall I say, Mitya?”

“Be silent!” cried Dmitri. “Wait until I’ve left. Don’t you dare, in my presence, to smear the good name of an honorable girl! That you should say a single word about her is an outrage, and I won’t allow it!”
He was gasping for breath.
“Mitya! Mitya!” cried Fyodor Pavlovitch in a hysterical voice, squeezing out a tear. “Does your father’s blessing mean nothing to you? What if I curse you?”
“Shameless hypocrite!” Dmitri shouted furiously.

“That’s how he talks to his father! His own father! Think how he treats other people! Gentlemen, just imagine. There’s a poor but honorable man living here, loaded down with a big family, a captain who got into trouble and was discharged from the army, though not in public, not by court-martial, and with no stain on his honor. Three weeks ago Dmitri grabbed him by the beard in a tavern, dragged him out into the street and beat him there in front of everyone. And all because the man is my agent in a little business of mine.”

“It’s all a lie! The outside is true, but the inside is a lie!” Dmitri was shaking with rage. “Father, I don’t defend what I did. Yes, I say it openly: I treated that captain like a brute. I’m sorry for it now, and I’m sick at myself for my brutal rage. But this captain, this agent of yours, went to that lady you call an enchantress. He suggested to her, from you, that she take my I.O.U.’s that you’re holding and sue me for the money, to get me thrown into prison with them, if I kept demanding an account of my property from you. And now you blame me for having a weakness for that lady, when you yourself pushed her to captivate me! She told me so to my face.... She told me the whole story and laughed at you.... You wanted to put me in prison because you’re jealous of me over her, because you’d started pressing your attentions on her. I know all about that too. She laughed at you for that as well—do you hear?—she laughed at you as she described it. And here he is, this man, this father, who reproaches his dissolute son! Gentlemen, forgive my anger, but I foresaw that this cunning old man would bring you together only to make a scandal. I had come ready to forgive him, if he held out his hand. To forgive him, and to ask his forgiveness! But he has just insulted not only me but an honorable young lady, whom I revere so much that I dare not speak her name carelessly. So I’ve decided to expose his game, though he is my father....”

He could not go on. His eyes glittered and he could hardly breathe. But everyone in the cell was shaken. All of them except Father Zossima rose from their seats, uneasy. The monks looked stern, but they waited for a lead from the elder. He sat still. He was pale, not from excitement but from the weakness of his illness. An imploring smile lit his face. From time to time he lifted his hand as if to calm the storm, and of course one gesture from him would have been enough to end the scene. But he seemed to be waiting for something, and he watched them closely, as though trying to make out something that was not entirely clear to him. At last Miüsov felt utterly humiliated and disgraced.

“We are all to blame for this scandalous scene,” he said heatedly. “But I did not foresee it when I came, though I knew who I was dealing with. This must be stopped at once! Believe me, your reverence, I had no exact knowledge of the details that have just come out. I did not want to believe them, and I am hearing them for the first time.... A father jealous over his son’s dealings with a woman of loose behavior, and plotting with the creature to get his son jailed! This is the company I’ve been made to sit in! I was deceived. I tell you all, I was deceived as much as anyone.”

“Dmitri Fyodorovitch,” Fyodor Pavlovitch suddenly yelled, in an unnatural voice, “if you weren’t my son, I’d challenge you right now to a duel ... with pistols, at three paces ... across a handkerchief,” he ended, stamping both feet.

Old liars who have spent their whole lives acting have moments when they slip so completely into the part that they shake or weep real tears, even though at that very moment, or a second later, they can whisper to themselves, “You know you’re lying, you shameless old sinner! You’re acting now, for all your ‘holy’ anger.”
Dmitri frowned painfully and looked at his father with indescribable contempt.

“I thought ... I thought,” he said, in a soft, almost controlled voice, “that I was coming home with the angel of my heart, my betrothed, to cherish his old age. And all I find is a depraved libertine and a despicable clown!”

“A duel!” the old wretch yelled again, gasping and spluttering on every syllable. “And you, Pyotr Alexandrovitch Miüsov, I’ll have you know that in all your family there has never been a loftier, or more honest—you hear?—more honest woman than this ‘creature,’ as you’ve dared to call her! And you, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, you’ve dropped your betrothed for that ‘creature,’ so you must have thought yourself that your betrothed couldn’t hold a candle to her. That’s the woman you call a ‘creature’!”
“Shameful!” broke from Father Iosif.
“Shameful and disgraceful!” Kalganov cried out in a boyish voice. He had said nothing until then, and now he flushed crimson and shook with feeling.

“Why is such a man alive?” Dmitri growled in a hollow voice, beside himself with rage, his shoulders hunched up so high that he looked almost deformed. “Tell me, can he be allowed to go on defiling the earth?” He looked around at them all and pointed at the old man. He spoke evenly and deliberately.

“Listen, listen, monks, to the parricide!” cried Fyodor Pavlovitch, rushing at Father Iosif. “There’s your answer to ‘shameful!’ What is shameful? That ‘creature,’ that ‘woman of loose behavior,’ may be holier than you are, you monks who are out to save your souls! She fell, perhaps, in her youth, ruined by the world around her. But she loved much, and Christ himself forgave the woman ‘who loved much.’”
“It was not for that kind of love that Christ forgave her,” the gentle Father Iosif broke in impatiently.
“Yes, it was, monks, it was for that kind! You save your souls here eating cabbage, and think you’re the righteous. You eat a gudgeon a day, and you think you can bribe God with a gudgeon.”
“This is intolerable!” was heard from all sides of the cell.

But this shameful scene was ended in the most unexpected way. Father Zossima suddenly rose from his seat. Alyosha was nearly frantic with worry for the elder and for everyone else, but he managed to hold him up by the arm. Father Zossima walked toward Dmitri, and when he reached him he sank to his knees. Alyosha thought he had fallen from weakness, but he had not. The elder bowed down at Dmitri’s feet, clearly and deliberately, until his forehead touched the floor. Alyosha was so astonished that he did not help him up again. There was a faint smile on the elder’s lips.
“Good-by! Forgive me, all of you!” he said, bowing to his guests on every side.

Dmitri stood for a few moments, amazed. Bowing down to him—what did it mean? Suddenly he cried out, “Oh, God!” He covered his face with his hands and ran from the room. The guests all streamed out after him, so confused that they did not say good-by or bow to their host. Only the monks went up to him again for a blessing.

“What did it mean, falling at his feet like that? Was it a symbol, or what?” said Fyodor Pavlovitch. He had suddenly gone quiet, and he tried to start the conversation again without daring to address anyone in particular. They were all just then leaving the grounds of the hermitage.
“I can’t answer for a madhouse and for madmen,” Miüsov answered at once, in a sour mood, “but I’ll spare myself your company, Fyodor Pavlovitch, and, believe me, for good. Where’s that monk?”

“That monk” was the one who had invited them to dine with the Superior, and he did not make them look for him. He met them the moment they came down the steps from the elder’s cell, as if he had been waiting for them all along.

“Reverend Father, would you do me a favor? Please give my deepest respects to the Father Superior, and apologize for me, Miüsov, in person to his reverence. Tell him I very much regret that, because of unforeseen circumstances, I can’t have the honor of sitting at his table, much as I would wish to,” Miüsov said to the monk, irritably.

“And that unforeseen circumstance, of course, is me,” Fyodor Pavlovitch cut in immediately. “Do you hear, Father? This gentleman doesn’t want to stay in my company, or he’d go right away. And you’ll go, Pyotr Alexandrovitch, please go to the Father Superior, and enjoy your meal. I’ll be the one to decline, not you. Home, home, I’ll eat at home. I don’t feel up to it here, Pyotr Alexandrovitch, my amiable relative.”
“I am not your relative and never have been, you contemptible man!”

“I said it on purpose, to drive you mad. You always deny we’re related, but you are, whatever your wriggling. I’ll prove it from the church calendar. Ivan, you stay if you like, and I’ll send the horses back for you later. Pyotr Alexandrovitch, it’s only proper for you to go to the Father Superior and apologize for all the disturbance we’ve been making....”
“Is it true you’re going home? You’re not lying?”

“Pyotr Alexandrovitch! How could I dare, after what’s happened! Forgive me, gentlemen, I got carried away! And upset, too! And honestly, I’m ashamed. Gentlemen, one man has the heart of Alexander of Macedon and another has the heart of the little dog Fido. Mine is the heart of the little dog Fido. I’m ashamed! After such an escapade, how can I go to dinner and gobble up the monastery’s sauces? I’m ashamed, I can’t. You must excuse me!”

“The devil only knows, what if he’s tricking us?” thought Miüsov. He hesitated, watching the retreating buffoon with suspicious eyes. The buffoon turned around, saw that Miüsov was watching him, and blew him a kiss.
“Well, are you coming to the Superior’s?” Miüsov asked Ivan sharply.
“Why not? I was specially invited yesterday.”

“Unfortunately I feel forced to go to this blasted dinner,” said Miüsov, with the same irritability, not caring that the monk was listening. “We ought at least to apologize for the disturbance, and explain that it wasn’t our doing. What do you think?”
“Yes, we should explain that it wasn’t our doing. Besides, father won’t be there,” Ivan said.
“Well, I should hope not! Blast this dinner!”

They all walked on, though. The monk listened in silence. On the path through the copse he made just one remark: the Father Superior had been waiting for a long time, and they were more than half an hour late. He got no reply. Miüsov looked at Ivan with hatred.
“Look at him, off to the dinner as if nothing had happened,” he thought. “A brazen face, and the conscience of a Karamazov!”
